oneSentence: A measure of how close two pieces of text are in meaning, even if they use different words.
plainExplanation:
Semantic similarity compares texts by meaning rather than by exact word overlap. The input is usually two texts, such as two sentences, a question and a paragraph, or a search query and many documents. The output is a score or ranking that shows which texts are closest in meaning.

A common way to do this is to turn each text into an embedding, which is a list of numbers designed to place similar meanings near each other. The system then compares those number lists and gives higher scores to items that are closer together. One common comparison method is cosine similarity, but semantic similarity is the broader idea, not the specific formula.

This matters because people often say the same thing in different words. A search for “flooded roads after storm” may still match a passage that says “transport routes were blocked after heavy rain”. Keyword search may miss that connection if the exact words do not overlap.

Semantic similarity does not prove that two texts are equally correct, complete or safe to use. It only estimates closeness of meaning based on patterns learned from data. That is why results still need checking, especially in high-stakes work.

everydayAnalogy.title: Finding the right note in a mixed pile
everydayAnalogy.story: Amina has a box of handwritten notes from colleagues in Nairobi, Bangkok and Bogotá about community meetings. One note says “parents asked for evening sessions”, another says “families prefer meetings after work”, and a third says “bring chairs to the hall”. She wants notes about the same idea, even when the wording differs, so she puts similar notes into the same tray. The first two notes end up together because they point to a similar meaning, while the chair note goes elsewhere.

mapping.aiElement: A system grouping or ranking texts by closeness of meaning
Texts that are semantically similar despite using different words

mapping.analogyElement: The chair note placed in another tray
mapping.aiElement: A text judged less similar because it expresses a different idea

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A person can use background knowledge and context that a system may not have, such as tone, irony or local customs. Real systems usually do not literally sort papers into trays. They compare mathematical representations of text, and their similarity scores can be wrong or biased if the training data or text context is weak.

visual.title: Word match versus meaning match
visual.learningObjective: Show why two texts can be close in meaning even when they do not share many words.
visual.description: A side-by-side comparison. The left panel shows keyword matching between a query and three passages, with only shared words highlighted. The right panel shows semantic similarity scores for the same query and passages, ranking the passage with closest meaning highest. Read from top to bottom in each panel, then compare the final rankings.

steps.label: Query
steps.explanation: Start with one search query or sentence to compare.
steps.visualInstruction: At the top centre, place a rounded box labelled 'Query: Roads blocked after heavy rain'.

steps.label: Keyword view
steps.explanation: Exact or near-exact word overlap is checked. A passage with few shared words may score low even if it means nearly the same thing.
steps.visualInstruction: On the left, draw three passage boxes under a heading 'Keyword search'. Highlight matching words in the same colour as the query. Show low, medium and high word-overlap badges.

steps.label: Meaning view
steps.explanation: Texts are compared by meaning. A passage can rank high even when the wording is different.
steps.visualInstruction: On the right, draw the same three passage boxes under a heading 'Semantic similarity'. Add score bars beside each passage, with the paraphrase passage receiving the highest bar.

steps.label: Result
steps.explanation: The best result under semantic similarity is the passage closest in meaning, not necessarily the one with the most shared words.
steps.visualInstruction: At the bottom, show two ranked lists side by side. Use arrows from each panel to its ranking. Mark the semantic result with a note 'best meaning match'.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each passage to reveal why it ranked where it did: shared words on the left, similarity score and short meaning note on the right.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram compares two ways of matching a query to passages. The query is 'Roads blocked after heavy rain'. In the keyword panel, passages rank mainly by shared words. A passage using different words, such as 'transport routes were closed after severe rainfall', ranks lower because few words match exactly. In the semantic panel, that same passage ranks highest because its meaning is closest. The main point is that meaning-based comparison can find relevant text even when wording changes.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static side-by-side graphic with the same query, passages, highlights and final rankings, without hover animation. Explanatory labels are always visible.

workedExample.scenario: A help-desk team wants to find past answers similar to a new question.
workedExample.input: New question: 'How can I reset my account password if I cannot receive the verification email?'
process: Three past tickets are compared to the new question.

Ticket A says 'Password reset link does not arrive in my inbox.' Ticket B says 'How do I change the language of the portal?' Ticket C says 'I cannot sign in because my badge access failed at the office gate.'
The system assigns semantic similarity scores: Ticket A 0.91, Ticket B 0.32, Ticket C 0.18.
Ticket A is ranked first because it is closest in meaning, even though it does not use exactly the same wording as the new question.
workedExample.result: The team reviews Ticket A first, then checks whether its past answer applies to the new question.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: After a disaster, an approved internal system compares short analyst notes about satellite imagery with earlier reports to find passages describing similar signs of washed-out roads, damaged bridges or temporary shelters.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: This helps staff find relevant prior assessments faster, even when teams in different locations use different wording for the same observed conditions.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Use only approved systems and approved data. Do not place confidential operational details, precise sensitive locations, personal data or protection-sensitive information into a public AI service.

whyItMatters: For non-specialists, semantic similarity matters because it affects what information you see first. If a system can match by meaning, it can find useful passages, past cases or reports that use different wording from your question. That can make search, support tools and retrieval-augmented generation more useful. But it also affects trust: a high similarity score does not mean a passage is correct, current or appropriate. Knowing this helps you ask better questions, check sources and avoid over-trusting a confident-looking result.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: It just means counting shared words.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Word overlap is a different method, often called keyword search. Semantic similarity tries to capture closeness of meaning, so two texts can score as similar even when they use different words.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A high similarity score means the answer is true.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The score only reflects estimated meaning closeness between texts. A passage can be very similar to your question and still be outdated, misleading or wrong, so human checking and source review still matter.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Semantic similarity and cosine similarity are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Semantic similarity is the overall concept of comparing meaning. Cosine similarity is one mathematical way to compare text representations such as embeddings. Systems may use cosine similarity, but the terms are not interchangeable.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: It is a way to estimate whether two pieces of text mean nearly the same thing, even when they do not use the same words.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In practice, semantic similarity is often estimated by encoding each text into an embedding, a numeric representation that places semantically related texts near one another in a vector space. A similarity function, often cosine similarity, is then used to score pairs of vectors. Higher scores suggest greater closeness of meaning. This supports tasks such as semantic search, retrieval and ranking. The exact behaviour depends on the embedding model, the text length, the domain, the language and the comparison method, so the score is an estimate rather than a proof of equivalence.

keyTakeaway: Semantic similarity helps systems find text with similar meaning, not just similar wording.

quickCheck.question: Which example best shows semantic similarity rather than simple keyword matching?
options: Matching 'car' with 'car' because the word is identical
Matching 'roads blocked after flooding' with 'transport routes closed after heavy rain' because the meaning is close
Matching the longest document because it contains more words
Matching a passage only because it was published most recently
quickCheck.explanation: The second option shows two texts with different wording but similar meaning. That is the main idea. Exact word overlap, document length and recency are different signals.

issues.problem: The phrase "a system to notice" presents the system as performing a human mental act. The mechanism estimates similarity from text representations rather than noticing meaning.
issues.fix: It is a way to estimate whether two pieces of text mean nearly the same thing, even when they do not use the same words.

issues.problem: The numerical ordering is correct: 0.91 > 0.32 > 0.18, so Ticket A ranks first. There is no other arithmetic to check. However, the example supplies only Ticket A's problem statement, not an answer or troubleshooting steps. The result therefore invents content that was never provided.
issues.fix: The team reviews Ticket A first, then checks whether its past answer applies to the new question.

issues.problem: The visual calls for three passages, overlap badges, score bars and two final rankings, but it provides the text of only one passage and no complete rankings. The accessibility description repeats an unsupported relative ranking without describing the other passages. Neither version gives enough information to render or verify the comparison.
issues.fix: Specify all three passage texts and their order in both rankings. Include the same passages and ranking order in the accessibility description. Use one close paraphrase, one high-overlap but different-meaning passage, and one unrelated passage.

issues.problem: The marked answer is the only best answer. Option 1 is both semantically related and an exact keyword match, but it does not demonstrate similarity rather than keyword matching. Options 3 and 4 are irrelevant ranking signals, so the answer is obvious without understanding the distinction.
issues.fix: Replace the distractors with plausible text-pair errors, such as "'Flood warning' with 'flood insurance' because both share 'flood'", "'Roads blocked' with 'roads repaired' because two words match", and "'Rain expected' with 'rain recorded' because one word matches".
